title: Appendix A. Input tables

Note (data transition WP01): the paths below refer to the original INPUT Tables/ locations, which are now under data_raw/tables/.
Review of INPUT Tables/Tables_SEN.xlsx and INPUT Tables/Tables_GNB.xlsx, 2026-09-19. Every sheet, row and cell was read. No input file was modified.

title: Appendix A. Input tables
text:
1. File layout
Both workbooks share one skeleton:

Header in row 1. No rows above it, no blank or section-header rows, no merged cells, no hidden rows, columns or sheets, no formulas, no comments.
Column A, indicator, holds one free-text label per row. It is the only row identifier; there are no indicator codes.
Every other column is named estimate<Group> and holds one value per indicator for that group.
Values are literal numbers already rounded to 2 decimals, with Excel number format 0.00.
Missing values are empty cells. No text, sentinel strings or error values appear in the numeric columns.
The rows are sorted by label in code-point order (so COICOP 10 comes before COICOP 1, and ≥1 HH member… is always last). The order carries no thematic meaning.
Both files were written by a script (creator = openpyxl in the file metadata). The 32-character cut-off in some column names matches Stata’s variable-name limit, so the tables most likely come from a Stata pipeline exported to Excel, but the file itself only proves the last step.

title: Appendix A. Input tables
text:
4. Value conventions

Shares are stored as 0–1 decimals, never 0–100, including labels that say “%”.
Levels are stored in the same columns as shares, with no unit or type field. A single number format cannot fit every row.
Values are rounded to 2 decimals at source. Anything below 0.005 is stored as 0.00 and cannot be told apart from a true zero.
An empty cell can mean either “not computed” (wood_dist) or “too few observations in this group” (scattered blanks in small regions). The file does not distinguish the two. Empty must not be read as zero.
Labels contain non-ASCII characters: en-dash – (15–64, Safe drinking water – dry season) and ≥. SDG is written both as SDG 7.1.1 and SDG7.1.1. Matching by typed text is fragile.

title: Appendix A. Input tables
text:
6. Discrepancies and data-quality issues

6.1 SEN Departement sheet

It contains the same 14 regions as ADM 1, spelled identically. There is no département-level data in the file.
It is an older or different version of the regional table:

Poverty is at 2017 PPP (Poor at $3.00/day (2017 PPP), Poor at $4.20/day (2017 PPP)) instead of 2021 PPP.
How far its values drift from ADM 1 varies by indicator. Six of the 60 shared indicators are identical (Employed (activ12m, 15–64), Employed in agriculture, Wage-employed, Non-wage employed, HH has internet access, Has health insurance/coverage (couvmal)). Most others differ modestly. The household-enterprise money variables differ heavily: up to 94% for HE revenue per worker, 68% for HE capital stock, 74% for HE costs, and 14.7x for HE profits.

Its indicator set does not match: 82 rows, 60 shared with the other sheets, 22 unique and 37 missing.

Unique rows include raw variable names: (max) con_1 … (max) con_15, (max) ext_emp, npoor300, npoor420.
Also unique: Access to electricity (grid or off-grid), Energy expenditure burden (share of total cons.).
Its 15 con_* consumption categories do not line up with the 13 COICOP rows elsewhere.

Some values are impossible:

HE has any credit access is 1.00 in all 14 regions (0.14–0.59 in ADM 1).
HE has formal credit access is 0.72–0.95 in every region (0.00–0.23 in ADM 1). HE has informal credit access looks unaffected (0.09–0.37, against 0.09–0.40 in ADM 1).
HH has 4+ HE is 0.80–1.00 in every region, although HH has 0/1/2/3 HE already sum to about 1 (at most 0.03 in ADM 1).




6.2 Issues in both countries







Issue
Evidence

wood_dist [ALL MISSING] has no values anywhere

Food consumption share = COICOP 1…; Housing & utilities burden… = COICOP 4… (identical values in every column)

Access to electricity (grid, SDG 7.1.1), Connected to electricity grid (SDG7.1.1) and Uses grid electricity differ by country: GNB national totals are 0.23 / 0.27 / 0.26, but SEN’s are 0.68 / 0.98 / 0.66, a 32-point spread. The definitions need documenting before any of the three is presented as “electricity access”


Rows with no variation at 2 decimals
COICOP 12 is 0.00 in every column of both countries. COICOP 9 is 0.00 in every column in SEN and on GNB National. COICOP 2 is 0.00 on SEN National and ZAE, and 0.01 in every column in GNB


Truncated column names
Names cut at exactly 32 characters (SEN Ziguinchor_Tamba_Kolda_S; GNB Zona_Plana_de_Centro_Bis, Zonas_Montanhosas_de_Les)


No geographic codes
Regions and zones are identified only by spelled names, and spelling conventions differ between countries

Average outage duration (code) is a mean of an ordinal code, not a duration

National estimateCapital is identical to ZAE estimateZonas_Costeiras_do_Sul on all 97 indicators. Against SAB, it matches on only 9 of 97, and all nine are rows that are constant everywhere anyway (wood_dist, COICOP 12, HE has external (non-HH) employees and similar). HE profits (FCFA) for TAMBACOUNDA is the only negative value in either country: −3,460 on ADM 1 and −50,754 on Departement, a factor of 14.7 apart. A loss-making average may be genuine, but it breaks any assumption that levels are non-negative, and the two tables disagree on its size.

title: Appendix A. Input tables
text:
7. Consistency checks that hold
Checked across every cell of both countries, and correct:

Poor at $3.00/day never exceeds Poor at $4.20/day.
Poverty falls monotonically from Q1 to Q5.
Regional values bracket the national value.
COICOP 1–13 sum to 0.96–1.02, which is what rounding 13 two-decimal shares produces.
Agriculture + industry + services, and food + non-food, sum to about 1; wage + non-wage sums to exactly 1.00.
HH has 0/1/2/3/4+ HE sums to about 1, except on SEN Departement.
HE has any credit access is at least as large as its formal and informal components, except on SEN Departement.

Two notes for anyone re-running these checks:

Scanning for identical columns or rows produces false positives. Some indicator pairs match only because both are near zero everywhere (for example GNB Owns wall AC/split and ≥1 HH member has health coverage). Require the values to vary before calling a pair a duplicate.
The duplicates in 6.2 pass that test: they track each other across the full range.

title: Appendix A. Input tables
text:
8. What harmonization will need

A long table with one row per country × breakdown × group × indicator, holding the value.
An indicator dictionary: stable code, label, theme, unit / value type, display format, poverty line, PPP year, source variable.
A geography lookup: admin code, level and display name for every region and zone, replacing name-based matching.
A way to mark missing values that separates “not computed” from “suppressed (small sample)”.
Fixes in the upstream pipeline, not the dashboard, for 6.1, the GNB Cultivated area (ha) outliers, the GNB Capital coding, and the constant or duplicate indicators.

title: SDMX conformance
text:
This page is the evidence that the AFW 360 files conform to the SDMX 3.1 family chosen in the standard (D27): SDMX-ML 3.1.0 for the structure message, SDMX-CSV 2.1.0 for data and reference metadata. Each row names a requirement, the command that checks it, and the result observed on 2026-09-29 on branch standard/v0.6-sdmx.
Commands run from the repository root in Git Bash. V is tools/verify/.venv/Scripts/python (Python 3.11, pysdmx[data,xml]==1.20.0, created by tools/verify/make_venv.sh or make_venv.ps1) and X is sdmx/structures/AFW360_structures.xml. The Python tools are for verification only and are never part of the R pipeline (D30). Rows 1 to 12 and 14 were rerun for this page; row 13 comes from the FMR run of the same day, whose reports are kept under tmp/fmr/ (gitignored).

title: SDMX conformance
text:
Notes on the evidence
Vendored schemas (row 1). pipeline/xsd/sdmx-ml-3.1/ holds the 30 files of schemas/ at tag v3.1.0 of sdmx-twg/sdmx-ml, entry SDMXMessage.xsd. The repository has no LICENSE, LICENCE or COPYING file at that tag and its README states no licence terms, so the folder’s README.md records the absence instead of quoting a licence. xml2::xml_validate() in build_sdmx.R and the validator’s SDMX.XSD check use the same schemas. pysdmx’s own read_sdmx(validate=True) validates against its bundled schemas, not these; xsd_validate.py covers the vendored ones.
pysdmx 1.20.0 limits (rows 8 and 12). pysdmx cannot read com:AnnotationValue, which the XSD allows and every codelist here uses; verify_sdmx.py validates the original bytes and hands pysdmx a copy without annotation values. It has no SDMX-CSV metadata reader (Format.REFMETA_SDMX_CSV_2_1_0 exists but no reader uses it), so the metadata messages get a header check: fixed columns, MDSTRUCTURE = metadataflow, TARGET_IDS naming an artefact of the message, and dotted headers whose last segment is an MSD attribute id. It does not check the parent prefix, MDSTRUCTURE_ID, TARGET_TYPES or the uniqueness of METADATASET_ID; the byte comparison of SDMX.STALE covers those. check_urns.py registers a maintainable without a version attribute (the organisation schemes) under version 1.0.
Legacy regression (rows 7 and 11). pipeline/reconcile.R matches every cell of the data files against the legacy workbooks (6871 cells OK, 98 GNB cells withheld by LEGACY_OVERRIDES.csv). The projection test in pipeline/tests/testthat/ maps each data file back onto the 31 columns of the previous layout and finds only the removed DATAFLOW column and NaN against empty on the 39 GNB O rows. Its comparator is unit-tested; the whole test has not been mutation-tested.
What the FMR round trip does not cover (rows 11 and 13). The MSD, the metadataflow and the metadata provision agreement are not in the 3.0 profile, so FMR neither loads nor exports them. import_sdmx.R does not write back the ARTEFACTS.csv columns status, version_added, notes, agency_id and source_file, edits to the derived codelists, AFW_METADATA_VERSION, the structure of the concept scheme, DSD, MSD, dataflow and agreements, non-English names, or sentinel names and their GLOBAL_CODE. The 3.0 profile keeps AnnotationValue, which FMR accepted; it has not been checked against the 3.0 XSDs.
FMR’s clean report. An FMR validation report says "Errors":false when the file is clean; the word “error” appears in a clean report, so the field, not a text search, is the test.

title: The SDMX standard in plain terms
text: SDMX (Statistical Data and Metadata eXchange) is the ISO standard that statistical agencies use to publish and exchange statistics. This page explains the few ideas behind it that matter for AFW 360.

title: The SDMX standard in plain terms
text:
How SDMX describes a number

Four kinds of column
In SDMX, one row of data holds one number plus everything needed to read it. Every column of that row is one of four kinds, which SDMX calls component types.



Table 1: The four SDMX component types










Component type
The question it answers
In our data




Dimension
What is this number about?
Country, region, urban or rural, indicator, poverty line, quintile, …


Time dimension

Measure

Attribute

Unit, status (estimated, missing, …), source, rounding






Three ideas follow from this:

The key. The dimensions and the time dimension together identify the number. No two rows may share the same key, so each combination of codes points to exactly one number.
Codelists. A dimension cannot hold free text, only a code from a fixed list. Rural is always R and the poverty rate is always POV_HC, in every country and every year.
Two reserved codes. _T means total, not split (all areas, both sexes). _Z means not applicable (no poverty line is needed for a food share). Every key cell is therefore always filled.

Swap R for _T and you get the national rate. Swap POVLINE_PL300 for POVLINE_PL420 and you get the rate at the higher line.
The values are shares between 0 and 1, never percentages. Each of these rows also carries the unit (SHARE), a status code and the source of the number, which are attributes and are not shown here.


Breakdowns and qualifiers
The dimensions in Table 2 do two different jobs. The standard calls them two families:

A breakdown says who is counted: rural households, the poorest quintile, people living in Fatick. Each category is a different part of the population.
A qualifier says what is measured: at which poverty line, in which PPP round, on which consumption category. Each category covers the same people again.

The quickest test is to ask whether the categories add up:

Breakdown: the parts add up to the whole. The five quintiles together are the whole population. Urban and rural together are the whole country. The national poverty rate is the population-weighted average of the urban and rural rates.
Qualifier: every category is the whole again. The $3.00 rate (0.18) and the $4.20 rate (0.37) describe the same Senegalese population, measured against two different lines, so they do not add up. Food (0.45), housing (0.17), transport (0.03) and the other COICOP divisions are all shares of the same households’ consumption, and the 13 of them sum to 1.

Three dimensions belong to neither family. They frame every number and are called reference dimensions: the frequency (always annual), the estimation method (survey or model) and the year.
Why the distinction matters:

Fewer indicators. There is one poverty rate, POV_HC, for every line and PPP round, not one indicator per line. There is one consumption share, CONS_SH, for all 13 COICOP divisions.
Automatic checks. Because the system knows which categories should add up, it can test the numbers. Regions must average to the national value, and COICOP shares must sum to 1.
Growth without new columns. A new grouping, such as sector of employment, or a new poverty line is a new code in a codelist. The file format does not change.

title: The SDMX standard in plain terms
text:
How SDMX stores the data

Two files
SDMX keeps the description of the data separate from the data itself (Figure 1):

The structure file (XML) is the dictionary. It defines every column, every allowed code and how they fit together. There is one per version of the standard, and every country shares it.
The data file (CSV) holds the numbers: one row per number, with its key codes, measures and attributes. There is one file per country, year and estimation method.

The two are linked by name. Every row of a data file says which dataflow it belongs to, in its STRUCTURE_ID column, and so which dictionary to check it against.






Figure 1: The structure file defines the columns and codes; the data file uses them. Each data row names its dataflow, and each code in it must exist in its codelist.



Descriptive information, such as survey details, data sources and the dashboard’s explanatory text, travels in further SDMX metadata files. They are left out of this page.


The structure file: why it looks complicated
The structure file is written in SDMX-ML, an XML format, and it is hard to read by eye. This has three causes:

Everything is wrapped in tags. Names, descriptions and notes each sit in their own element, in several languages if needed.
Everything has a full identity. Each item carries an agency, an id and a version, for example WB.AFW360:CL_URBANISATION(0.3.0).
Everything refers to everything else by that identity. Items are never simply named. A single column of the data file is spread across several places that point to one another.

Take the URBANISATION column. First, the codelist lists its allowed values. The extract below is shortened: each code also carries notes such as its status and the global code it matches.
<str:Codelist agencyID="WB.AFW360" id="CL_URBANISATION" version="0.3.0">
  <com:Name xml:lang="en">Degree of urbanisation</com:Name>
  <com:Description xml:lang="en">Urban and rural areas of residence, with the
    capital city and other urban areas as children of urban.</com:Description>
  <str:Code id="U">
    <com:Name xml:lang="en">Urban</com:Name>
  </str:Code>
  <str:Code id="R">
    <com:Name xml:lang="en">Rural</com:Name>
    <com:Description xml:lang="en">The area is rural.</com:Description>
  </str:Code>
  <!-- CAP (capital city), OU (other urban), _T (total) -->
</str:Codelist>
Next, the data structure definition declares the column as a dimension. It does not repeat the name or the codes. It points to the concept that says what the column means and to the codelist that says which values it takes:
<str:Dimension id="URBANISATION">
  <str:ConceptIdentity>urn:sdmx:org.sdmx.infomodel.conceptscheme.Concept=WB.AFW360:CS_AFW360(0.3.0).URBANISATION</str:ConceptIdentity>
  <str:LocalRepresentation>
    <str:Enumeration>urn:sdmx:org.sdmx.infomodel.codelist.Codelist=WB.AFW360:CL_URBANISATION(0.3.0)</str:Enumeration>
  </str:LocalRepresentation>
</str:Dimension>
Finally, the dataflow gives the dataset a name and points to the data structure definition. Repeat this for 34 columns and 22 codelists, and the file runs to thousands of lines.
The benefit is that a machine can check everything. With the structure file alone, any SDMX tool knows which columns a data file must have, which codes each column accepts and what type each value must be. Nobody has to write those checks by hand.
Nobody writes it by hand either. The structure file is generated from the standard’s plain CSV dictionaries, one table per codelist. Those tables are what people edit.

title: The SDMX standard in plain terms
section: Writing SDMX from R or Stata
text:
Writing SDMX from R or Stata

The tools gap
Full SDMX support exists mainly in Java and Python. The Java library behind the Fusion Metadata Registry (FMR) and Python packages such as pysdmx and sdmx1 can read, write, validate and convert every SDMX format, including the XML.
R and Stata have no such writer. Their SDMX packages, such as rsdmx in R and sdmxuse in Stata, are built to download data from statistical agencies, not to produce SDMX files. Yet most country economists compute their indicators in R or Stata.
The workaround is SDMX-CSV. Instead of writing SDMX-ML, a producer writes an ordinary CSV table laid out the way SDMX-CSV requires. Any R or Stata user can do that with the commands they already know (write.csv(), export delimited). The CSV is a complete, official SDMX format, so it is also the intermediate step to everything else. FMR or pysdmx can validate it against the structure file and, if a user ever needs it, convert it to SDMX-ML or SDMX-JSON without losing anything.


What SDMX-CSV is
SDMX-CSV is the CSV format defined by the SDMX standard itself. We use version 2.1, which belongs to SDMX 3.1. It is a flat table with one row per observation and one column per component of the data structure definition. Each column header is the component’s id (REF_AREA, INDICATOR, OBS_VALUE, …), and each cell holds a code from the matching codelist, never a label. Three fixed columns come first. STRUCTURE and STRUCTURE_ID say which dataflow, and which version of it, the rows belong to. ACTION says what a receiving system should do with each row, for example R to replace any earlier value.
What makes a plain CSV into SDMX is that link to the structure file. The CSV holds no definitions of its own. A tool reads STRUCTURE_ID, fetches that dataflow’s data structure definition, and from it knows which columns are dimensions, measures or attributes, which codes are allowed, and which data types apply. It can then check every row and build any other SDMX format from the table. Missing values follow fixed conventions: an empty cell means not provided, and NaN marks a number that is intentionally missing. A file written this way is therefore readable by people, easy to produce from R or Stata, and fully machine-checkable.

title: The SDMX standard in plain terms
text:
In short

One row is one number. Its dimensions and year say what it is, its measures say how much and how reliable, and its attributes say how to read it.
Among the dimensions, breakdowns say who is counted and qualifiers say what is measured.
SDMX stores this as two files: an XML dictionary, generated and shared by all countries, and a CSV of numbers, one per country, year and estimation method. Each row of the CSV names the dictionary it follows, so any SDMX tool can check it.
R and Stata cannot write SDMX-ML, so producers write SDMX-CSV: a plain CSV laid out to the standard, which SDMX tools then validate and, if needed, convert to any other SDMX format.

title: Step 1: From Excel tables to SDMX data
text: Two Excel workbooks, one per country (Tables_SEN.xlsx and Tables_GNB.xlsx), made to be read by people, not by machines. Rows carry free-text labels, each column is a group (“Total”, “Capital”, “Dakar”, …), the two countries are laid out differently, and nothing says what a number is: a share or a count, its unit, its survey or its year.

Rows carry free-text labels, each column is a group (“Total”, “Capital”, “Dakar”, …), the two countries are laid out differently, and nothing says what a number is: a share or a count, its unit, its survey or its year.

title: Step 1: From Excel tables to SDMX data
text:
The problem in one sentence
To make a standard, every number needs a full “address”: what was measured, where, for whom, how and when. In the Excel files that address is only implied by where the number sits on the sheet.

title: Step 1: From Excel tables to SDMX data
text:
What we did

We wrote the structure ourselves. We did not start from an outside template. We built the structure from what we already knew about the indicators, their groupings and the geography, and from what the dashboard needs to show. It breaks every number’s address into separate parts (dimensions in SDMX terms):

country and region, written as official region codes instead of names;
indicator, for example the poverty rate or livestock ownership;
who the number describes: sex, age, urban or rural, and other groupings such as consumption quintile or the sex of the household head;
qualifiers of the measure, such as the poverty line used;
year and method (survey or model).

Each number also carries a few notes (attributes in SDMX): its unit, its status (for example “empty in the Excel file”) and its source. How this structure was designed is explained in The SDMX standard for AFW360.
We wrote down how the Excel files map to that structure. Each Excel column and each row label is matched to its place in the structure in a few small CSV tables (metadata/plans/) that anyone can read and review. The mapping is kept in these tables, not inside the code. For example:







In the Excel file
In the standard




Sheet National, column “Capital”
whole country, area = capital city


Sheet ADM 1, column “DAKAR”
region = Dakar (code SN01)


Row “Access to electricity (grid)”
indicator = EN_ELEC_ACCESS



We converted the files with one script. pipeline/convert_legacy.R reads the Excel files and writes one standard data file per country, survey and year. The Excel files are never edited, and every value in the output can be traced back to its sheet and cell.

  A["Excel tables<br/>(unchanged)"] --> C["Conversion script"]
  B["Mapping tables<br/>(CSV, reviewable)"] --> C

title: Step 1: From Excel tables to SDMX data
text:
What we got

Two data files, AFW360_HH_SEN_2021_SURVEY.csv and AFW360_HH_GNB_2021_SURVEY.csv, in one shared format: the same column names and the same codes for both countries.
The dashboard now reads only these files. Moving to them uncovered mistakes that the Excel layout had hidden; for example, the Guinea-Bissau page was showing Senegal’s numbers.

title: Step 1: From Excel tables to SDMX data
text:
What we learned

The structure is our best reading of the tables, not a final answer. Every code is still marked as a draft.
Some information was never in the Excel files and cannot be recovered, such as standard errors and sample sizes. Those fields are left empty and marked as missing.
Turning the tables into data forced decisions the Excel files left vague, for example what counts as “other urban”. Each decision is recorded in the data standard.

title: Step 1: From Excel tables to SDMX data
text:
What comes next

The structure is formalised as an SDMX standard (a Data Structure Definition with its code lists) in The SDMX standard for AFW360.
The converted data is then checked against that standard (Step 3).

title: Africa West 360: High-level overview
text:
This page is the map of the whole (ideal) process of data transformation for the Africa West 360 (AFW360) project. The goal of AFW360 is to operationalize microdata for daily use by country economists and analysts through:

enabling access to the raw microdata as is using an API.
harmonizing microdata with clear harmonization guidelines and data provenance and enabling API-based access to it.
creating a reproducible pipeline of indicators creation from the harmonized microdata and enabling access to those through an API.
making indicators operational for humans and AI through a dashboard, a data access MCP server, and AI chats.

This is a concept note with a few prototypes to prove the concept.


Our starting point is a set of Excel files produced from the raw data. It gives an overview of a fragment of the pipeline as well as the initial version of the dashboard developed by Moritz Meyer and published here: https://datanalytics-int.worldbank.org/AFW360-v1/ (requires VPN to access). Original data and dashboard code are located in the folder 10-legacy-pipeline/. Figure 1 shows how they connect.






Figure 1: Legacy Pipeline






Our goal is to create a sustainable data transformation pipeline, where data provenance is transparent and the produced indicators are accessible to machines and humans and could be operationalized in the future as:

statistical data,
an API,
an MCP server for search and extraction by AI,
a basis for AI processing and for building stories based on the data.

Figure 2 shows the ideal pipeline: a medallion-style (Bronze, Silver, Gold) ETL (extract, transform, load) pipeline. It is designed to be modular, with each stage building on the previous one.






Figure 2: Ideal Pipeline



Bronze. Raw microdata ingestion and operationalization through an API-like sustainable access interface. The World Bank (WB) has several systems for this, each with its own strengths and limitations. The main ones are:

Development Data Hub: https://datacatalog.worldbank.org/. This appears to be the best of the available options. It permits hosting data in individual files without the need for deep standardization, gives access to the data through streamable APIs and integrates directly with Databricks and other data storage platforms. It is the way of publishing data for analysis recommended by the WB reproducibility team.
World Bank Microdata Library: https://microdatalib.worldbank.org/index.php/home. This is another option used to disseminate microdata. Its key limitation is that it requires exhaustive preparation of the data and metadata, which is costly. As a result, its coverage is patchy, and data are often available only as incomplete data sets.
Datalibweb: https://datalibweb2.worldbank.org/home. A Stata-native system designed for hosting and serving the Global Monitoring Database (GMD). It benefits from granular access control, but the way it serves data to users is restrictive and is harder to use outside Stata.

Silver. Harmonization of microdata into a common format, with clear documentation of the harmonization decisions and a reproducible data pipeline. This stage establishes a shared harmonization standard across countries and regions and enables API-based dissemination of the harmonized data. As a dissemination platform, the Development Data Hub could be used again, or the World Bank Microdata Library could share the harmonized data with standard documentation, in the same way as the Global Labor Database (GLD) is shared: https://microdatalib.worldbank.org/index.php/catalog/GLD/
Gold. Production of indicators in a standard SDMX format in a fully reproducible manner that enables data access for the final users.
There are a few concepts here worth exploring:

SDMX (Statistical Data and Metadata eXchange): a standard for statistical data and metadata exchange. It is widely used in the international statistical community and supported by many statistical software packages and visualization tools. It is the standard behind WDI, OECD Stats, Data 360 and other data dissemination platforms. It matters because it makes data provenance transparent and reproducible and communicates clearly what the computed indicators and data are.
SDMX data files: access to SDMX data is simple for analysts. Each country, survey and year is represented as a single CSV file with supporting metadata. Users load it into their statistical software and start working with it. These files could be hosted on the Microdata Library or the Development Data Hub.
API: an API is the standard way to access SDMX-based data because it gives every user (people, statistical software and so on) the same interface for reading and loading data. One example is the Data 360 API https://data360.worldbank.org/en/int/api. Type https://data360api.worldbank.org/data360/indicators?datasetId=WB_WDI in the browser and you will get the full list of indicators available in the WDI database.
MCP server (Model Context Protocol server): software that lets local or remote AI agents communicate with the API and extract data from it. It is what connects any AI agent to the data and metadata. Data 360 introduces its MCP server here: https://worldbank.github.io/data360-mcp/, and it is used across AI agents. It is open source and could be adopted at low cost. MCP servers are powerful because they can be integrated into the World Bank’s internal AI chats, mAI and k360, enabling data exploration augmented by access to WB knowledge and internal documentation.
AI chat: probably the final stage of the process. It operationalizes AI to answer development questions based on the data and metadata available for the region in SDMX format. One prototype is https://data360.worldbank.org/en/int/chat; another is https://k360.worldbankgroup.org/ (requires VPN to access). Both use a set of MCP servers to access relevant information. They use AI to rephrase the questions (prompt engineering) so that they retrieve the most relevant data and structure the answers well.
Dashboards: the human-oriented interface to the data. Having data structured as an SDMX database with an API enables any dashboard to be built on top of it and deployed through channels such as Power BI, Tableau and R Shiny.
Supporting knowledge: a key element of a successful and relevant data pipeline. For AI to give relevant, data-supported answers to development questions, it needs to know how to reason. This is why a hierarchy of supporting knowledge is important: the development questions, the data and the metadata. It gives AI correct references and templates for reasoning, for exploring the data and for writing the answer. In practice, this knowledge is structured plain text organized so that AI can use it, e.g. AI Skills.

This pipeline could be implemented in any statistical software, but its advantages show most in a scalable working environment such as Databricks. We could also borrow implementation best practices from the GLD.

Bronze. Raw microdata ingestion and operationalization through an API-like sustainable access interface. The World Bank (WB) has several systems for this, each with its own strengths and limitations. The main ones are:

Development Data Hub: https://datacatalog.worldbank.org/. This appears to be the best of the available options. It permits hosting data in individual files without the need for deep standardization, gives access to the data through streamable APIs and integrates directly with Databricks and other data storage platforms. It is the way of publishing data for analysis recommended by the WB reproducibility team.
World Bank Microdata Library: https://microdatalib.worldbank.org/index.php/home. This is another option used to disseminate microdata. Its key limitation is that it requires exhaustive preparation of the data and metadata, which is costly. As a result, its coverage is patchy, and data are often available only as incomplete data sets.
Datalibweb: https://datalibweb2.worldbank.org/home. A Stata-native system designed for hosting and serving the Global Monitoring Database (GMD). It benefits from granular access control, but the way it serves data to users is restrictive and is harder to use outside Stata.

Silver. Harmonization of microdata into a common format, with clear documentation of the harmonization decisions and a reproducible data pipeline. This stage establishes a shared harmonization standard across countries and regions and enables API-based dissemination of the harmonized data. As a dissemination platform, the Development Data Hub could be used again, or the World Bank Microdata Library could share the harmonized data with standard documentation, in the same way as the Global Labor Database (GLD) is shared: https://microdatalib.worldbank.org/index.php/catalog/GLD/
Gold. Production of indicators in a standard SDMX format in a fully reproducible manner that enables data access for the final users.
There are a few concepts here worth exploring:

SDMX (Statistical Data and Metadata eXchange): a standard for statistical data and metadata exchange. It is widely used in the international statistical community and supported by many statistical software packages and visualization tools. It is the standard behind WDI, OECD Stats, Data 360 and other data dissemination platforms. It matters because it makes data provenance transparent and reproducible and communicates clearly what the computed indicators and data are.
SDMX data files: access to SDMX data is simple for analysts. Each country, survey and year is represented as a single CSV file with supporting metadata. Users load it into their statistical software and start working with it. These files could be hosted on the Microdata Library or the Development Data Hub.
API: an API is the standard way to access SDMX-based data because it gives every user (people, statistical software and so on) the same interface for reading and loading data. One example is the Data 360 API https://data360.worldbank.org/en/int/api. Type https://data360api.worldbank.org/data360/indicators?datasetId=WB_WDI in the browser and you will get the full list of indicators available in the WDI database.
MCP server (Model Context Protocol server): software that lets local or remote AI agents communicate with the API and extract data from it. It is what connects any AI agent to the data and metadata. Data 360 introduces its MCP server here: https://worldbank.github.io/data360-mcp/, and it is used across AI agents. It is open source and could be adopted at low cost. MCP servers are powerful because they can be integrated into the World Bank’s internal AI chats, mAI and k360, enabling data exploration augmented by access to WB knowledge and internal documentation.
AI chat: probably the final stage of the process. It operationalizes AI to answer development questions based on the data and metadata available for the region in SDMX format. One prototype is https://data360.worldbank.org/en/int/chat; another is https://k360.worldbankgroup.org/ (requires VPN to access). Both use a set of MCP servers to access relevant information. They use AI to rephrase the questions (prompt engineering) so that they retrieve the most relevant data and structure the answers well.
Dashboards: the human-oriented interface to the data. Having data structured as an SDMX database with an API enables any dashboard to be built on top of it and deployed through channels such as Power BI, Tableau and R Shiny.
Supporting knowledge: a key element of a successful and relevant data pipeline. For AI to give relevant, data-supported answers to development questions, it needs to know how to reason. This is why a hierarchy of supporting knowledge is important: the development questions, the data and the metadata. It gives AI correct references and templates for reasoning, for exploring the data and for writing the answer. In practice, this knowledge is structured plain text organized so that AI can use it, e.g. AI Skills.

This pipeline could be implemented in any statistical software, but its advantages show most in a scalable working environment such as Databricks. We could also borrow implementation best practices from the GLD.

text:
What we did

We moved everything old into one folder, 10-legacy-pipeline/. All the original files now live in one place, apart from the new work. Nothing inside the files was changed.
We locked the original data. The Excel tables, maps, texts and picture are in a subfolder called data_raw/. A “fingerprint” of every file is stored next to them, so anyone can check that not a single byte has changed. The stray test files sit in a separate corner that nothing uses.
We brought in the working online dashboard. A colleague had already rebuilt the dashboard as an interactive web app. We copied it into the same folder and pointed it at the locked original data.
We checked that it works. The app’s automatic checks all pass, it opens correctly on a test computer, and the older static web page still builds next to it.
We set it up to publish to the World Bank’s internal web server (Posit Connect). It sends only the files the app needs and leaves behind the large map files and the test files.

Limitations

The original data contain errors and inaccuracies (see Appendix A). For example:

In Guinea-Bissau, the column labelled “Capital” holds the figures of a different zone.
In Guinea-Bissau, cultivated land is reported in the millions of hectares for some groups, which is impossible.
Some indicators are empty, show the same value everywhere, or repeat others.
Senegal’s file includes an older regional table that disagrees with the main one and contains impossible values.

text: The file sdmx/structures/AFW360_structures.xml is an SDMX-ML 3.1 structure message. It is generated by pipeline/build_sdmx.R from metadata/, so you never edit it by hand. Its core is the Data Structure Definition (DSD) WB.AFW360:DSD_AFW360_HH(0.3.0). Everything else in the file either feeds the DSD or points at it.

title: Step 2: Establish an SDMX Data Structure Definition (DSD) for our indicators
text:
What a DSD does
A DSD is the schema for every number in data/*.csv. It says three things:

Which columns identify an observation (the dimensions, together called the “key”).
Which columns hold numbers (the measures).
Which columns describe a number without identifying it (the attributes).

It also ties each column to a concept (its meaning, in CS_AFW360) and to a representation: either a codelist of allowed values or a plain type such as Double or String. That is why every country file has the same 37 columns, with the same codes in them.

The main design choice is the two groups of five “slot” dimensions:

COMP_BREAKDOWN_n splits the population: by quintile, decile, sex or age of the household head, poverty status, employment sector, and so on.
MEASURE_QUAL_n changes the definition of the indicator: which poverty line, which PPP round, which welfare concept.

Slots are filled left to right in a fixed slot_order. This keeps the key the same width for every indicator: adding a new kind of breakdown or qualifier means adding codes to a codelist, not changing the DSD.
The two “nothing” codes mean different things:

_T means “total”, i.e. not broken down.
_Z means “not applicable”. For example, SEX=_Z on a household-level indicator.

title: Step 2: Establish an SDMX Data Structure Definition (DSD) for our indicators
text:
2. Measures: the numbers (9)
The DSD uses SDMX 3.x multiple measures, so one row can carry a value and its precision statistics:

OBS_VALUE is mandatory. It is unrounded and in base units, so rates are shares between 0 and 1. It is NaN when OBS_STATUS is O or M.
The other eight are optional (minValue="0" where a negative value makes no sense):

STD_ERR, CI_LOWER, CI_UPPER: sampling error and the 95% confidence interval.
N_OBS, N_POP, N_OBS_NUM: unweighted records, weighted population, and numerator records for shares.
DEFF, DF: design effect and degrees of freedom.


They are optional in the DSD, but the project validator requires them on PRODUCER-source rows. Today’s rows all come from converting the legacy workbooks, so these columns are empty.

What each AttributeRelationship means:

SERIES_ID depends only on the “what and how” dimensions, not on country, area or year. It is the readable series name the dashboard matches on. It is a plain string, not a codelist, because SDMX IDs cannot contain dots.

Fusion Metadata Registry 12.4.2 rejects SDMX-ML 3.1, so this DSD is loaded into FMR with --sdmx-ml-version 3.0. The DSD loads, but the MSD, the metadataflow and the metadata provision agreement are left out, so the metadata files are not checked in FMR.
To change the DSD, edit metadata/structure/DSD_AFW360_HH.csv (named in the AFW_SOURCE_FILE annotation) and regenerate the XML with build_sdmx.R.

title: AFW 360 data standard and producer guidelines
text:
This document defines how data for the West Africa Micro Data 360 platform (AFW 360) are structured, coded and documented, how producers create data files, and how the database is extended to new countries, indicators and breakdowns. It follows the SDMX information model (the ISO standard statistical agencies use to exchange data) and borrows the World Bank Data360 dimension layout, stored as plain CSV files in git.
Background on the current inputs is in input-tables-findings.qmd. Nothing here changes the legacy inputs under data_raw/. An R converter produces the new files from them (transition.qmd), and the Python dashboard reads them through the loader package afw360 (D37); the SDMX conformance evidence is on sdmx-conformance.qmd and the FMR workflow on fmr-guide.qmd.
How to read this document. Section 1 is the whole idea on one page: the model, where every file lives, and how the database grows. Read it first. Sections 2 to 12 are reference material; come back to them when you need the exact rule. Section 13 records the design decisions already taken and those still open. Table 1 suggests where to start.
Every table in this document that lists the contents of a metadata file is generated from that file by pipeline/build_docs.R and included from .docs/generated/ (Section 11.1). Those tables cannot drift from the metadata; the prose around them can, and is what to fix if the two disagree.

text:
1.1 One row is one number
Each row of a data file carries one value and the full set of codes that say what that value is: which country, which year, which population, which measure. Those codes fall into two families (Table 2), and telling them apart is the whole model.

The quickest test is the population. If the people behind the categories add up to the whole, as regions or quintiles do, the variable is a breakdown. If every category covers the same whole population again, as the $3.00 and $4.20 poverty lines do, it is a qualifier. N_POP, the population behind each row, makes the test mechanical.
This matters for three reasons. The poverty rate at any line and PPP round is one indicator, POV_HC, not one per line. Every population share is one of three indicators — POP_SH (individuals), POP_HH_SH (households) or POP_HE_SH (enterprises), chosen by what the breakdown counts (D4) — not thirty. And a new grouping such as sector of employment is a row in a codelist, not a change to the file format.
The indicator, its qualifiers and, for a share, the category it is a share of together name a series: “poverty headcount at $4.20 (2021 PPP)” or “share of employed persons working in agriculture”. Every series is one row of SERIES_PLAN.csv, with a stable series_id and a display name, and every data row carries its SERIES_ID (D13). The series is what dashboards, reports and readers think in; the indicator and qualifier codes are how a series is built.
This distinction is the foundation of the database. Every rule in the rest of this document follows from it, and everyone who adds data has to apply it consistently.

title: AFW 360 data standard and producer guidelines
text:
1.3 Where everything lives
Everything is plain files in one git repository, in ten top-level folders (Listing 1):

data_raw/ holds the current legacy inputs, byte-frozen: file names and bytes unchanged, proven by data_raw/CHECKSUMS.sha256 (D2).
pipeline/ holds the R code that reads data_raw/ and the plans and writes every other folder: the metadata bootstrap, the converter, the validator and the SDMX generator and importer (D1, D11, D30).
metadata/ is the dictionary. It says what every code means, which rows a data file must contain, which rules the numbers must satisfy, and which surveys and program runs the numbers come from. Every other folder refers to it, and every change to it is reviewed (Section 11).
data/ holds the numbers: one CSV per country, reference year and estimation method, each with a manifest recording how it was produced and against which metadata version.
geo/ holds the boundaries used for maps.
content/ and assets/ hold the prose and images the dashboard shows beside the numbers.
sdmx/ holds the SDMX-ML structure message and the SDMX-CSV metadata messages, generated from metadata/ and content/, committed and checked for staleness (D28, Section 3.10).
tools/ holds tools outside the pipeline: the independent SDMX verification in Python (tools/verify/, D30) and the FMR install notes and scripts (tools/fmr/, D35).
afw360/ is the Python package of the dashboard loader, the one place the dashboard reads data from (D37).

Until producers deliver files, the converter does their job: it turns the current Excel tables into data files using LEGACY_LABELS.csv (Annex).
Metadata is generated once, then frozen (D11). The first version of every file under metadata/ was generated by an R script in pipeline/bootstrap/, from hand-written seed tables (pipeline/bootstrap/seeds/*.csv) and a small authored text file (pipeline/bootstrap/text/*.csv). Structural migrations are scripts, run once (D12). When a release changes the columns of a metadata file or of the data file, the change is made by a script under pipeline/migrations/<version>/, committed with the release and run once. The script reads the previous version’s files and writes the new ones, so the change is reviewable and reproducible; it never re-runs the bootstrap. After it has run, hand editing resumes.
The metadata, the converter and the validator exist, and the two countries’ files have been produced from the legacy workbooks (transition.qmd). The dashboard reads them through the loader in afw360/ (D37); no chunk of index.qmd reads data_raw/ any more (Section 7.3).
The 0.3.0 migration (pipeline/migrations/0.3.0/migrate.R) is the worked example of that rule. It refuses to run unless VERSION is the previous release, and it reads authored inputs from pipeline/migrations/0.3.0/inputs/ (the artefact list, the DSD rows, CL_FREQ.csv, COLUMNS_0.3.0.csv, CHANGELOG_0.3.0.md and the alignment table), so the script itself holds no hand-typed names or descriptions. Its choices where the plan was silent: ALIGNMENT.csv has the columns codelist, code_0_2_0, code_0_3_0, name_en, definition_en, global_urn, and an empty name_en or definition_en keeps the previous value (an added code, today only CL_UNIT_MEASURE.XOF, fills both); XOF is appended as the last row of CL_UNIT_MEASURE.csv with status DRAFT; a code rename also rewrites parent and replaced_by references in the same list; the CL_FREQ rows of the alignment table are checked against inputs/CL_FREQ.csv, not applied; in COLUMNS.csv the CL_FREQ block comes before CL_SEX and the ARTEFACTS.csv block after the COLUMNS.csv rows. With --out-root <dir> it writes a complete metadata tree, and diff -r against the committed metadata/ is empty.

title: AFW 360 data standard and producer guidelines
text:
1.4 How the database grows
The rule for every extension is metadata first, data last. A number can enter the database only once its codes exist, so every change starts in the codelists and ends with a data file that the validator accepts. If a new number cannot be described with the existing codes, the codes are extended first, in the same pull request as the data.
A new country is added in this order:

Register the country in CL_AREA.
Register its spatial schemes in CL_GEO_SCHEME and their units in CL_GEO.
Check its indicators against the dictionary, CL_INDICATOR. Every country should produce the same set of indicators, matching the dictionary’s codes, definitions and meaning. When a country’s survey cannot match a definition, update the dictionary with a new code linked to the old one through related, rather than stretching an existing code to fit.
Do the same for breakdowns and qualifiers: the country’s categories map to the shared codes in CL_COMP_BREAKDOWN and CL_QUALIFIER.
Describe the survey in SURVEYS.csv, and add the boundary files the maps need.
Produce the data file for each reference year, following TAB_PLAN, together with its manifest.

Section 8.4 gives each step in full.
A new indicator starts in the microdata, not in the aggregation. First standardize the variables it needs in the survey microdata itself, so that each one has the same definition, universe, unit and recall period in every country. Once they are standardized, the indicator is a simple aggregate of them: a mean, a share or a total over each cut. If an indicator needs complicated logic at the aggregation step, its variables are not yet standardized enough.
Every constructed variable also needs its own metadata, recording what the microdata looked like when the indicator was computed from it: the questionnaire module and questions, the recall period, the universe, the units and any recoding. CL_INDICATOR points to these variables through source_questionnaire, source_vars and program. Where the variable-level documentation itself is kept is still an open decision (Section 13.2).
Everything else, such as a breakdown, a qualifier, a poverty line, a spatial scheme, a survey round, a piece of text or a figure, is listed in Table 30 with the files to edit and the version bump it needs. The only structural change is to the columns of the data file, and only the data team makes it (Section 11).

Fixed columns. SDMX-CSV requires them in every message. They are not components of the DSD and are not rows of DSD_AFW360_HH.csv.

STRUCTURE is always dataflow.
STRUCTURE_ID is WB.AFW360:AFW360_HH(<VERSION>), with the content of metadata/VERSION: today WB.AFW360:AFW360_HH(0.3.0).
ACTION is R on every row (D38, Section 2.6).

The DATAFLOW column of metadata version 0.2 is gone: STRUCTURE_ID names the dataflow and its version.
The key is the 18 dimensions plus TIME_PERIOD, 19 columns, FREQ through TIME_PERIOD. Together they identify one observation, and no two rows of the database share them. FREQ is the first dimension and is always A, annual, coded by CL_FREQ (D34).
Measures (D33). An observation carries nine measures. OBS_VALUE is the value itself and is mandatory. STD_ERR, CI_LOWER, CI_UPPER, N_OBS and N_POP were attributes in metadata version 0.2 and are now measures; their meaning is unchanged (Section 2.6). Three optional measures are new: N_OBS_NUM, the unweighted number of records in the numerator of a share; DEFF, the design effect; and DF, the degrees of freedom of the variance estimate. None of the three can be derived from the others, and all matter for reliability. N_OBS_NUM is required where STD_ERR is; DEFF and DF are optional until a producer file defines them. Legacy files leave every measure but OBS_VALUE empty.
Attributes. Six attributes describe the observation. Each is attached at a stated level:

SERIES_ID is attached to INDICATOR and the ten breakdown and qualifier dimensions, and UNIT_MEASURE to REF_AREA and INDICATOR. Both are repeated on every row and have exactly one value per combination of those dimensions across all data files; the validator checks this (STRUCT.ATTR_LEVEL, Section 12).
PRECISION, OBS_STATUS, SOURCE_ID and OBS_COMMENT are attached to the observation. OBS_STATUS also relates to the measure OBS_VALUE.
SERIES_ID, UNIT_MEASURE, OBS_STATUS and SOURCE_ID are mandatory and never empty (D39). PRECISION and OBS_COMMENT are optional.

Four of the attributes were added in metadata version 0.2 so that a row can be read without opening any other file (D13 to D16):

SERIES_ID names the series the row belongs to (Section 6.12). It is redundant with the key, and the validator checks that they agree. It is an uncoded String: series ids contain ., which SDMX code ids forbid, so no codelist is derived from SERIES_PLAN.csv, and the validator checks every value against that file instead (D43, Section 6.1).
UNIT_MEASURE is the unit of OBS_VALUE, resolved for the country: SHARE, PERSON, HA or, for money, the ISO 4217 currency code such as XOF (Section 2.6). All of them are codes of CL_UNIT_MEASURE, which was called CL_UNIT before version 0.3.0 and now lists the currency codes too (Section 3.8).
PRECISION is the rounding unit of OBS_VALUE in base units, empty when the value is exact. A legacy conversion of a share rounded to two decimals writes 0.01; a count converted from millions rounded to two decimals writes 10000.
SOURCE_ID names the program run that produced the row, in SOURCES.csv (Section 6.15). Its codelist CL_SOURCE is derived from that file (D43).

title: AFW 360 data standard and producer guidelines
text:
2.2 The two sentinels
_T and _Z are reserved codes with fixed meanings. They are never listed in a codelist CSV, and no code in any codelist CSV may start with _. The SDMX generator adds them to the generated codelists, because SDMX validators accept only values that exist in the codelist (D42, Section 6.1).

_T, total. The value covers every unit and is not split on this dimension. Valid in GEO, SEX, AGE, URBANISATION and the breakdown slots.
_Z, not applicable. Valid in every unused qualifier slot, and in SEX or AGE when the indicator is not about individuals. A household-level indicator writes SEX=_Z, not SEX=_T, because “total over both sexes” would be a claim about a dimension that does not apply to households.
GEO and URBANISATION are never _Z: every unit lives somewhere.

Three further SDMX sentinels are reserved and not yet used (D21): _U unknown, _O other, and _X not allocated. They exist so that a classification with a residual category can still be a partition that sums to one. No breakdown variable has such a category today; when one does, it uses these codes rather than inventing OTHER or UNKNOWN categories.

title: AFW 360 data standard and producer guidelines
text:
2.3 Estimation method
ESTIMATION is a key dimension that says how the value was produced (D17), with the codes of CL_ESTIMATION:

SURVEY: a direct estimate from the survey microdata of the reference year.
MODEL: a model-based value for the reference year, whether a nowcast, a projection or a microsimulation, built on an earlier survey or on scenario assumptions.

The two can coexist for the same country and year, for example a 2026 nowcast built on the 2021 survey next to the 2026 survey estimate once it exists. Because ESTIMATION is part of the key, the two never collide, and a chart can overlay them. They live in separate files, named AFW360_HH_<ISO3>_<YEAR>_<ESTIMATION>.csv, each with its own manifest and its own source in SOURCES.csv, which records the base survey and the program.
Every row of a MODEL file carries OBS_STATUS=E unless the cell is empty (O) or cannot exist (M). Which series a MODEL file must contain is declared in SERIES_PLAN.csv’s estimation column (Section 6.12); a nowcast typically covers poverty and inequality only.

title: AFW 360 data standard and producer guidelines
text:
2.4 Rules for the breakdown columns

Fill the slots from the left, with no gaps. Unused slots are _T.
Use the canonical order. When a row has several breakdowns, they go in ascending slot_order from CL_BRK_VAR, with ties broken alphabetically by var_code. Each combination then has exactly one spelling.
One category per variable per row.
Respect unit compatibility. A breakdown variable may be used only with indicators whose stat_unit appears in its applies_to_units.
Never duplicate a named dimension. Residence, individual sex, individual age and geography always go in their own columns.
SEX and AGE describe the individual being counted, not the household head. The head’s characteristics are breakdown variables (HHH_SEX, HHH_AGE) and go in the slots.
An age band that defines an indicator’s universe is not a breakdown. “Employed, 15–64” has that band in its universe and writes AGE=_T.

title: AFW 360 data standard and producer guidelines
text:
2.5 Rules for the qualifier columns

Fill from the left, with no gaps. Unused slots are _Z.
Use the canonical order: ascending slot_order from CL_QUAL_VAR, with ties broken alphabetically.
One category per qualifier variable per row.
A row may use only the qualifiers its indicator declares in INDICATOR_QUALIFIERS.csv (Section 6.14), plus any qualifier required by a breakdown it uses. POOR_Y requires a poverty line, so a food-share row broken down by poverty status carries POVLINE_* and PPP_* even though CONS_SH does not otherwise use them.
Pairings must be allowed: QUALIFIER_PAIRS.csv says which PPP rounds go with which line (Section 6.14).

title: AFW 360 data standard and producer guidelines
text:
2.6 Values and attributes

Store OBS_VALUE unrounded, with . as the decimal separator and no thousands separator or % sign. Rounding is a display decision (display_as, decimals).
Use base units. Shares are 0–1, never 0–100. People are counted in persons, not millions. Money is in whole currency units.
UNIT_MEASURE repeats the indicator’s unit_measure on every row, so the file can be read without the dictionary (D14). The dictionary stays country-neutral: a money indicator has unit_measure = LCU there, and the data row resolves it to the country’s currency from CL_AREA, so a Senegal row says XOF. Every other unit is copied as is. The validator checks the two agree.
PRECISION is empty for a value written unrounded, which is every value a producer delivers (D15). Only a conversion from an already-rounded source fills it, with the rounding unit in base units: 0.01 for a share rounded to two decimals, 10000 for a count that was published in millions with two decimals. The validator’s tolerances and the dashboard’s display cap read it (Section 7.3).
SOURCE_ID names the program run that produced the row, registered in SOURCES.csv (D16, Section 6.15). A file may hold rows from several sources, for example poverty from one program and fiscal incidence from another; the manifest lists them all.
Do not suppress. Every estimate is published whatever its sample size. Reliability travels with the value instead: N_OBS and N_POP are required on every row, STD_ERR and the confidence interval on every row whose statistic admits them, and the dashboard shows them (Section 7.3). A value that rests on too few records is flagged OBS_STATUS=U, not hidden (below).
N_OBS is the unweighted number of records of the estimation file used: records in the group, in the indicator’s universe, with a non-missing value. When a person-weighted poverty rate is computed on a household file, N_OBS counts households. SURVEYS.analysis_units records which file each stat_unit is estimated from, so a reader always knows what N_OBS counts.
N_POP is the sum of weights over those same records: the population, households or enterprises the value refers to.
On a share row, both counts are the denominator (D19). “Share of employed persons working in agriculture, poorest quintile” is estimated as a mean over employed persons in the quintile, and N_OBS and N_POP are the records and weighted population of that universe, not of the agricultural workers. The group is the population cut, quintile; the defining breakdown, sector, is what is measured. The agricultural workers’ own population is OBS_VALUE × N_POP by definition, so it is not stored. The partition checks of Section 12 therefore run over population cuts only, never over a series’ defining breakdown.
Standard errors and confidence intervals must reflect the survey design (weights, strata and PSUs, with linearized variance). Intervals are at 95%.
Rows from a legacy conversion carry PRECISION and no reliability measures, because the workbooks hold neither. The exemption is a property of the source: the reliability columns are required on every row whose source has kind = PRODUCER, and may be empty where it has kind = LEGACY_CONVERSION (Section 7.2).
Missing values (D39). OBS_VALUE is NaN on every row whose OBS_STATUS is O or M, and a number on every other row. NaN is the SDMX-CSV value for an intentionally missing float or double; #N/A, the value for every other type, is not used. An optional measure or attribute that the source cannot supply is left empty, which SDMX-CSV reads as “not provided”. The mandatory attributes SERIES_ID, UNIT_MEASURE, OBS_STATUS and SOURCE_ID are never empty.
ACTION is R (replace) on every row of a published file (D38). R replaces whole observations and merges attributes above observation level; it does not delete observations missing from the file. A consumer that replaces a slice deletes it first, so a published file contains no D rows (Section 3.2).

OBS_STATUS takes one of the codes in Table 5, which come from the SDMX cross-domain CL_OBS_STATUS. A cell that can never exist is normally declared in the indicator’s excluded_breakdowns (Section 6.2) and left out of the file. M covers such a cell when it has not been declared there: the row stays, with OBS_VALUE = NaN, so the gap is visible.

Two of the codes are set by a rule rather than by judgement (D22):

U, low reliability, applies when N_OBS is below the dataflow’s minimum, or when the coefficient of variation STD_ERR / |OBS_VALUE| exceeds the dataflow’s maximum for a statistic that admits a standard error. Both thresholds are rows of RULES.csv with scope DATAFLOW (RELIABILITY_MIN_NOBS, initially 30, and RELIABILITY_MAX_CV, initially 0.30). The producer writes the code, and the validator recomputes it and reports a mismatch as an error. A row with no N_OBS and no STD_ERR, as in a legacy conversion, is never U.
D, definition differs, applies to every row of a series that a country produces with a definition that departs from the dictionary’s. It is allowed only where SERIES_PLAN.csv has a row for that country and series with status = DEVIATES (Section 6.12), and is required on every row of such a series.

One code per row. When several apply, the first of M, O, E, D, U, A in that order is written. A model-based value that would also fail the reliability rule is therefore E, and its standard error stays visible for the reader’s own judgement. Q, suppressed, is registered so that the code exists if a statistical office’s confidentiality rule ever has to be honoured; nothing in the database uses it today, and the no-suppression policy stands.

title: AFW 360 data standard and producer guidelines
text:
2.7 Which rows exist
plans/SERIES_PLAN.csv is the explicit list of series to produce: one row per series_id, naming its ref_area, INDICATOR, the qualifier combination in MEASURE_QUALS and, for a share indicator, the category it is a share of in DEFINING_BREAKDOWN (Section 6.12). A plain Cartesian product of qualifiers over cut categories over-generates — CONS_SH crossed with COICOP and poverty status gives 39 combinations where only 15 are real — so SERIES_PLAN states the real ones instead.
A series row with ref_area = ALL applies to every country. A row for a specific country overrides the ALL row for the same series_id and carries that country’s status: NOT_PRODUCED when the survey cannot support the series, in which case no rows are required, or DEVIATES when the country produces it under a definition that departs from the dictionary’s, in which case the rows are required and carry OBS_STATUS=D (D23). The estimation column says in which kind of file the series is expected, SURVEY, MODEL or both.
For each applicable SERIES_PLAN row whose estimation includes the file’s ESTIMATION and whose status for the country is not NOT_PRODUCED, the required data rows are:

(the cuts in TAB_PLAN compatible with the indicator’s stat_unit, found through CL_BRK_VAR.applies_to_units rather than a unit column on TAB_PLAN itself — geography and urbanisation cuts apply to every unit) × (the categories of those cuts) − (anything listed in excluded_breakdowns) − (cells withheld in LEGACY_OVERRIDES.csv)

The coverage generator writes SEX=_Z and AGE=_Z, not _T, wherever TAB_PLAN says sex = _T / age = _T but the indicator’s stat_unit is not IND (Section 2.2). It also keeps each generated row’s provenance — its cut_id and defining breakdown — so that a check such as “the parent of a row” (Section 12) is computed from that provenance rather than guessed from the row’s codes in general.
Nothing extra, nothing missing. A cell with no observations is a row with OBS_STATUS=O, not an absent row. This is what makes a file checkable: the validator can compute the set of rows that should exist and compare it with the rows that do.
A cell known to be wrong is different again: it is withheld, not published. Its row is absent from the file, the exclusion is registered in metadata/plans/LEGACY_OVERRIDES.csv (action WITHHOLD, with a reason and evidence), and the coverage check reads the register and subtracts it from the required rows (D5). Action COMMENT is not a withholding: the value is kept, OBS_COMMENT is set, and the row still counts as required.

title: AFW 360 data standard and producer guidelines
text:
3.1 Identity and versioning

Agency. Every artefact is maintained by WB.AFW360, a sub-agency of the registered World Bank agency WB (D31).
Agency scheme. The project ships a WB:AGENCIES agency scheme (fixed id, no version attribute in XML) that declares one agency, AFW360, named “West Africa Micro Data 360 (AFW DIP/POV team)”. It is a local placeholder so that WB.AFW360 resolves in FMR, pysdmx and the XSD and URN checks. It asserts nothing in the World Bank’s namespace and is never submitted to any registry. At registration it is replaced by the World Bank’s own scheme. Before loading into a World Bank registry, check whether WB:AGENCIES already exists there; if it does, have AFW360 added to it and drop the local copy. Global registration is a later step, taken by the World Bank’s SDMX owner.
Version. Every maintainable artefact carries agencyID="WB.AFW360" and version="0.3.0", the content of metadata/VERSION (D40).
Semver dependency rule. A semver artefact references only semver artefacts (IM technical notes, Annex “Semantic Versioning”, “Dependency Management”; the XSD does not enforce it). The one exception is a reference to an item of the fixed-version organisation schemes, AGENCIES, DATA_PROVIDERS and METADATA_PROVIDERS, whose URN version is (1.0). The XSD requires those references, and the SDMX.URN check exempts them. Annotation values such as GLOBAL_CODE and SDMX_CROSS_DOMAIN_CONCEPT are not structural references.
URN form. urn:sdmx:org.sdmx.infomodel.<package>.<Class>=WB.AFW360:<ID>(0.3.0). A code appends .<CODE>.
Short reference form, used in CSV messages: WB.AFW360:<ID>(0.3.0).
Message header sender id: WB_AFW360. Sender ids are plain IDs and cannot contain a dot.
Artefact ids are NCNames: a letter, then letters, digits, _ or -. The project code rules (Section 6.1) are stricter and stay.
Released artefacts are immutable. A released X.Y.Z never changes (SDMX semantic versioning). Edits between releases are made on a -draft copy and re-imported into the CSVs; the next release bumps VERSION and regenerates every artefact (D40, Section 11).

Rules:

37 columns, in the order of the DSD file’s position column (D46): the three fixed columns, the 18 dimensions, TIME_PERIOD, the nine measures, then the six attributes. The key is the 18 dimensions plus TIME_PERIOD, 19 columns (Section 2.1). The header is one physical line.
STRUCTURE is always dataflow. STRUCTURE_ID is WB.AFW360:AFW360_HH(<VERSION>).
ACTION is R, replace, in every published file (D38). The SDMX-CSV 2.1 guide recommends R for complete query responses; I and A are deprecated. R replaces whole observations and merges attributes above observation level. It does not delete observations missing from the file. A consumer that replaces a slice deletes it first, with a D row of the partial key REF_AREA, ESTIMATION, TIME_PERIOD. The published files contain no D rows.
FREQ is A.
Missing values (D39). OBS_VALUE is NaN when OBS_STATUS is O or M, and a number otherwise. NaN is the SDMX-CSV intentionally-missing value for float and double components only. #N/A is the value for every other type and is not used. Optional measures and optional attributes are left empty when not available; in SDMX-CSV, empty means “not provided”. The mandatory attributes SERIES_ID, UNIT_MEASURE, OBS_STATUS and SOURCE_ID are never empty. The validator enforces the rule through VALUE.NUMERIC (which accepts NaN) and VALUE.STATUS_EMPTY (an error on NaN or empty under a status other than O or M, and on a number under O or M). It still accepts an empty OBS_VALUE on an O or M row as missing, because older coverage tests build such rows; enforcing “NaN only” is left to a later validator change. The published files carry NaN on every such row.
Attributes on partial keys. SERIES_ID and UNIT_MEASURE are attached to partial keys, replicated on every row, and carry exactly one value per partial key across all data files: SERIES_ID per INDICATOR and the ten breakdown and qualifier dimensions, UNIT_MEASURE per REF_AREA and INDICATOR. The validator check STRUCT.ATTR_LEVEL (ERROR) groups all rows of all files by each attribute’s relationship dimensions and reports any group with more than one distinct value.
Numbers use . as the decimal separator and no thousands separator.
Encoding. RFC 4180 quoting, written with readr::write_csv(..., na = ""), so readr’s default NA never appears. UTF-8 without BOM, LF line endings. LF is a project convention and a documented deviation from RFC 4180, which specifies CRLF; the SDMX-CSV 2.1 guide does not address line endings or BOM.
File names are unchanged: AFW360_HH_<ISO3>_<YEAR>_<ESTIMATION>.csv.
Manifest. The key dataflow becomes structure_id and keeps its slot; a new key sdmx_csv_version, holding 2.1.0, follows it; the other 15 keys keep their order, 17 keys in all (Section 6.10). The validator reports a wrong value of either key as COVER.MANIFEST, with row key key=structure_id or key=sdmx_csv_version. The manifest stays a project-level sidecar; it describes a file, which is not an SDMX artefact.

3.4 Codelists and the CSV-to-SDMX mapping
Every metadata/codelists/CL_*.csv becomes a codelist WB.AFW360:CL_*(0.3.0). Columns map to SDMX by convention, with no mapping file to maintain (D41). The mapping is mechanical and reversible, which the FMR round-trip needs.
